title: A King Renews His People's Promise
overview: After a major victory, a prophet urges King Asa to stay loyal to God, and Asa leads Judah in clearing out idols and renewing their commitment.

parts.label: A prophet meets the king (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Asa is coming home from winning a war (told in chapter 14), and a prophet named Azariah meets him with a reminder rather than praise. The core message is that God stays close to those who stay close to him, and the victory is no guarantee if they turn away.

parts.label: A lesson from hard times (vv. 3-7)
parts.note: Azariah describes a period when the people had no real knowledge of God, no priests teaching them, and constant violence, yet God answered when they turned back. Scholars are unsure which period he means: perhaps the chaotic era before Israel had kings, perhaps the northern kingdom of his own day, or possibly a warning about the future.

parts.label: Idols removed, crowds gather (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Encouraged, Asa clears idols from his land, repairs the main altar at the temple, and calls an assembly that includes many people who had moved south from the rival northern kingdom. The gathering in the third month likely matched the harvest festival later called Pentecost, and the animals offered came from the war plunder.

parts.label: A solemn national promise (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: The people swear together, with shouting and trumpets, to seek God with their whole being, and they agree that anyone who refuses will be put to death. This harsh penalty reflects laws in Deuteronomy against worshiping other gods, and the text presents the oath as joyful and followed by peace.

parts.label: Removing the queen mother (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Asa strips Maakah of her official title as queen mother (the Hebrew word can mean mother or grandmother) because she set up an image of Asherah, a goddess of the surrounding peoples, and he burns it in the valley east of Jerusalem. The local hilltop shrines remained, which seems to clash with 14:3, and scholars explain this in different ways, such as these being shrines in the north or ones he failed to remove later.

parts.label: A long peace (v. 19)
parts.note: There is no war until Asa's thirty-fifth year. This date is hard to fit with the timeline in 1 Kings, and scholars have not settled how to reconcile them.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the warning that God will forsake those who forsake him states a lasting principle for individuals today or applied specifically to ancient Israel's covenant as a nation.
think: Can a shared commitment be truly wholehearted when refusing it carries a heavy penalty?
